Davenport is a storm-damage town

Local measurements and geology — not national boilerplate.

August 10, 2020 is the reference event: a derecho crossed Iowa with winds over 100 mph along its track, gusting 86 mph at Davenport Municipal Airport and 79 mph at the Quad City International Airport, knocking out power to 111,546 Quad-Cities households and causing roughly $11 billion in damage across the Midwest — the costliest thunderstorm in U.S. history. Davenport's city arborist called the local tree losses “uncountable,” and silver maple — the dominant big tree in the city's older neighborhoods — was the most frequently downed species. Storms like that don't just take trees; they leave thousands of cracked limbs and half-failed crotches that come down in the next ordinary thunderstorm.

Sources: National Weather Service / KWQC derecho wind surveys; Quad-City Times (outage count); NOAA ($11B damage estimate)

The right order of operations after a storm

First, people and power: if a tree or limb is touching any wire, stay away and call the utility before anyone else — a tree energized through a service drop can be lethal, and no tree crew will touch it until the line is dealt with. Second, if the tree is on the house, get people out from under the damaged section and photograph everything before cleanup — your insurer wants to see the tree where it landed, not a stump and a woodpile.

Then the tree work: a crew stabilizes what is hanging, gets the weight off the structure with rigging or a crane, tarps what is opened up, and clears access. Not every storm-damaged tree is a removal — a healthy tree that lost a limb can often be pruned and kept. What should never be kept is a hanger: a cracked limb resting in the canopy, waiting for the next wind. Walking the yard for hangers after a big blow is the cheapest storm insurance there is.

  • Trees on structures — rigged or craned off, then tarped
  • Hangers and cracked limbs removed before they finish falling
  • Documentation-friendly: work sequenced so your insurance photos exist
  • Blocked driveways and access cleared first

Davenport Emergency & Storm Tree Service — FAQ

A tree is on my house right now. Who do I call first?
If any wire is involved: the utility, full stop. Otherwise: your insurer's claim line and a tree crew, in either order — but photograph the scene before anything is moved. Emergency mitigation (getting the tree off and the hole covered) is generally covered work; full cleanup is sorted with the adjuster after.
Does homeowners insurance pay for storm tree removal?
Usually yes when the tree hit a covered structure — the removal-from-the-structure and repairs are typically covered, subject to your deductible, and policies often cap the removal portion. A tree that fell harmlessly in the yard is frequently not covered. Your policy's wording controls; the photos you take before cleanup are what make the claim smooth.
What does emergency work cost compared to planned work?
More — crane time, night or weekend response, and working a loaded, unpredictable tree all add real cost, and storm demand spikes prices regionally. That is exactly why the hazard trees worth worrying about are cheaper to remove on a calm Tuesday than during the week after a storm.
Can you save a tree that lost a big limb?
Often, yes. If the break is clean, the remaining structure is sound, and less than roughly a third of the canopy is gone, proper pruning cuts let the tree compartmentalize the wound. A trunk split down the middle, or a leader torn out, usually cannot be saved. An honest crew will tell you which one you have.
